title: What is cloud computing? A complete guide
seoTitle: What Is Cloud Computing? IaaS, PaaS and SaaS Explained
seoDescription: Learn how cloud computing works, the main service and deployment models, benefits, trade-offs, security responsibilities and when cloud makes sense.
excerpt: Cloud computing turns computing, storage, databases and software into services that can be provisioned on demand.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Cloud computing provides IT resources on demand through shared or dedicated infrastructure operated as services.
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS move different amounts of operational responsibility from the customer to the provider.
Public cloud can improve speed and elasticity, but cost, architecture, security and vendor dependence still require active management.
Cloud is an operating model, not a guarantee that every workload will be cheaper or more reliable.
body: Cloud computing changed infrastructure from something organizations primarily bought and installed into something they can provision through APIs. A team can create compute, storage, networking or managed databases in minutes instead of waiting for physical hardware.
The important idea is not simply that servers live somewhere else. Cloud combines pooled infrastructure, automation, self-service, metering and elastic capacity into a service model.

sections.heading: How cloud computing works
paragraphs: Cloud providers operate large fleets of servers, networks and storage systems across data centers. Virtualization and software-defined infrastructure divide those physical resources into services customers can request programmatically.
Customers choose regions, services and capacity while the provider operates the underlying facilities. The exact responsibility boundary depends on the service being consumed.

sections.heading: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
paragraphs: Infrastructure as a Service gives customers relatively low-level building blocks such as virtual machines, networks and disks. The customer still manages operating systems and applications.
Platform as a Service moves more responsibility to the provider by offering managed runtimes, databases or application platforms. Software as a Service delivers the finished application itself.
bullets: IaaS: maximum infrastructure control, with more operational responsibility.
PaaS: managed platform components that reduce infrastructure work.
SaaS: a finished application consumed by users.

sections.heading: Public, private and hybrid cloud
paragraphs: Public cloud services run on infrastructure owned by a cloud provider and shared through strong logical isolation. Private cloud applies cloud-like automation and self-service to infrastructure dedicated to one organization.

Hybrid environments combine cloud services with private or on-premises systems. This is common when organizations have regulatory requirements, existing data centers, latency constraints or systems that are difficult to migrate.

sections.heading: Why companies use the cloud
paragraphs: Cloud can shorten the time between an idea and usable infrastructure. Teams can automate environments, scale capacity and use managed services that would be expensive to build independently.
It can also shift spending from large hardware purchases toward usage-based operating costs. That flexibility is useful, but poorly governed cloud environments can become surprisingly expensive.
bullets: Fast provisioning through APIs and infrastructure as code.
Access to managed databases, analytics, AI and other higher-level services.

sections.heading: Security and the shared responsibility model
paragraphs: Moving to cloud does not outsource all security. Providers secure parts of the physical infrastructure and managed service, while customers remain responsible for areas such as identities, permissions, data, application vulnerabilities and configuration.
Misconfigured access policies and exposed credentials can therefore create serious incidents even when the underlying cloud platform is operating correctly.

sections.heading: Cloud cost and vendor lock-in
paragraphs: Usage-based pricing makes experimentation easy, but persistent resources, data transfer, premium managed services and overprovisioning can create high bills. Mature teams use tagging, budgets, rightsizing and FinOps practices to understand where money goes.
Managed proprietary services can accelerate development while making migration harder. The correct balance depends on whether portability or speed of delivery matters more for a particular workload.

sections.heading: When cloud is the right choice
paragraphs: Cloud is attractive when organizations value rapid provisioning, variable capacity, managed services and global reach. It is less automatically compelling for stable workloads already running efficiently on owned infrastructure or where strict latency, sovereignty or cost constraints dominate.
A good cloud strategy starts with workload requirements rather than a blanket assumption that everything belongs in one environment.

faq.question: Is the cloud just someone else's computer?
faq.answer: That phrase captures the remote-infrastructure idea but misses automation, managed services, elasticity, metering and global service delivery that distinguish modern cloud platforms.

faq.question: Is cloud always cheaper than on-premises infrastructure?
faq.answer: No. Cost depends on utilization, architecture, staffing, data transfer, purchasing models and the workload. Cloud often improves flexibility, but it still requires cost management.

faq.question: What is serverless computing?
faq.answer: Serverless services let developers run code or applications without directly managing servers. Infrastructure still exists, but more operational responsibility is handled by the provider.
